1440155,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.1.1.1.1,1946-08-17,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Mr. G. B. ISNOR (Halifax) presented the fifth and final report of the special committee on war expenditures and economies, as follows:
The special committee on war expenditures and economies begs leave to present the following as its fifth and final report.

Under date of March 22.1946, your committee was appointed ""to examine the expenditures defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for national defence and demobilization, and for other services directly connected with the war. including the disposal of surplus war assets, and to report what, if any. economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government, may be effected therein.""
The committee met four days after its appointment and since that date it has held forty-one sittings and heard twenty witnesses.
A steering committee was set up and recommended procedure which was approved by the main committee.

In giving consideration to matters coming within the scope of its reference, your committee decided to pursue the inquiries initiated during the last session, and accordingly turned its attention towards the operations of War Assets Corporation, its organization, functions and policies in the marketing of surplus assets, its priority system, etc. It also inquired into the methods of declaring surpluses, and the receiving, checking, and storing of such surpluses before final disposal.

Arising out of these inquiries, it rvas found expedient to secure evidence from the three armed services, viz.: navy, army and air force with a view to ascertaining what quantities of material and equipment had been transferred to War Assets Corporation for disposal and whether, in the interest of economy, stocks held by these services are limited to their requirements under post-war establishments.
A visit was made to the head office of War Assets Corporation, at Montreal, so that firsthand information could be sought and a study made of the general organization and set-up of the corporation.

Before the committee had proceeded at any length into the study of quick disposals it was felt that a change in respect of priorities should be given consideration, so that the disposal of surplus material could be effected with greater expedition by revising the method of granting priorities insofar as the time element was concerned. It wras, therefore, recommended and approved by the house ""that in respect of priorities granted to federal, provincial and municipal governments, the thirty day period now- in effect, be reduced to ten days.""

From the evidence submitted it w'as ascertained that greater care should be exercised by the armed services and War Assets Corporation wdien surpluses w'ere being turned over, and. accordingly your committee recommended, and the house approved, ""that when surpluses are to be declared by the armed services, or from any other source, advance notice be given to War Assets Corporation so that a representative of the corporation be on hand to cheek and receive surpluses.""

Your committee desires to draw to the attention of the house, and particularly to the attention of the Minister of Defence, that in prewar days there were 93 personnel carrier vehicles and that the post-war requirements show 4,133 vehicles of this type, which number appears excessive.

Witnesses from the Royal Canadian Air Force also appeared before the committee and gave a general outline of the policies and practices affecting equipment during the latter years of the war, since the cessation of hostilities, as well as those in effect at the present time.

The statement dealt with all forms and types of equipment, provisioning and contract cutbacks, stock retentions, disposal policy and other matters of policy. In connection with declared surpluses, it was shown that the air force had declared, as at May 1, 1946, equipment of an approximate total cost of $624,677,000.

Considerable discussion centred around the destruction of material at Penhold, Calgary and other depots. A statement was submitted which did not meet with general approval. The committee, as a whole, was critical of the manner in which the R.C.A.F. admittedly acting under general authority from War Assets Corporation, had brought about the destruction of equipment at these R.C.A.F. depots. This equipment, which was termed unserviceable (i.e., beyond economical repair) and had been listed as of no marketable value, was marked for physical destruction.

It is to be regretted, and is indeed unfortunate, that no collective statistical data was kept of the equipment which was reduced, to produce as it was not apparent at the time that there was any advantage to be gained from the additional administrative work involved. It was pointed out by the R.C.A.F. that all serviceable bits and pieces and parts were extracted. The destruction, nevertheless, took place; and although the policy, in this respect has been changed, your committee take the definite stand that no such procedure or action should have been followed or allowed. According to R.C.A.F. witness no further destruction has taken place since August, 1945.

Witnesses were also heard from the special service branches of the navy and air force and from the joint services advisory committee on welfare, voluntary and auxiliary services, Department of National War Services, respecting donations of materials, equipment and furnishings for the comfort and enjoyment of men and women of the services and the final disposal of same, by sale or otherwise.

Your committee recommends that such donated equipment, materials and furnishings above referred to and still in stores, be disposed of and that the revenue derived from this source be used for the benefit of the personnel of the armed services.

Because of articles appearing in newspapers and magazines respecting the destruction of war materials, it was deemed advisable to call before the committee the writer of certain of these articles which charged the air force with the alleged mutilation and scrapping of batteries delivered from No. 1 Equipment Depot, Toronto. The writer of those articles made what appeared to your committee serious charges against the air force and War Assets Corporation. One of his statements was that, while he had not counted the number of batteries on a junk pile he figured the volume of one battery, and then using a correcting factor, arrived at a number of 2,000. The R.C.A.F. witness stated that only 371 batteries had been released from No. 1 Equipment Depot from 25th June, 1945, to October 3, 1945.

Another allegation by the same witness was to the effect that he had purchased for $5 a damaged 5J22 battery, which cost the taxpayers §80. This statement w'as contradicted and invoices produced to show that this type of battery (5J22) cost the taxpayer only $14.68.

Certain other figures of costs as submitted by this writer witness were challenged, and figures of actual cost were given to show the incorrectness of statements contained in printed articles, although the great majority of figures of cost have not yet been examined.

Your committee's inquiry in this connection had not reached a stage where further comment on the evidence can be made, but your committee feels that what appear to be sensational articles, should not go unchallenged.
Another subject which your committee had under consideration and to which it devoted much time and study, is the question of making war surpluses available for instructional and school purposes.

Witnesses were heard in support of a more generous treatment to educational institutions. The policy and procedure whereby War Assets Corporation disposes of surplus material and equipment to educational institutions were submitted to the committee. These dealt very fully with all phases of this important question, and members of the committee gave careful attention to means whereby useful equipment could be made available to educational institutions with the least possible delay. While, in the opinion of your committee the present policy of indefinite loan is sound from the viewpoint of War Assets Corporation, your committee recommends:

column2: That the present policy of indefinite loan to educational institutions be broadened to include equipment not readily saleable.
That official educational representatives be permitted to visit and inspect such material and equipment as may be considered of educational value.
That there be granted to educational institutions a discount equal to that received by any dealer for similar lines.

column1: In the interest of economy, it is further recommended that additional outlets be found, or other suitable steps taken, with a view to speeding up War Assets Corporation's sales, and thus save storage and maintenance charges and. at the same time, place much needed material on the market.
The following measures are also recommended to speed disposal, viz.:

column2: Decentralized ""sales-at-the-site"";
Selecting ""short-supply"" civilian items for immediate sale;
Disposing of real property as quickly as possible, consistent with the protection of public interest;
Making all building material immediately available for construction purposes;

column1: [Mr. Isnor.l

column2: The non-employment by War Assets Corporation of persons otherwise interested in outside business;
Greater publicity by War Assets Corporation in respect of the sale and disposal of all war surpluses.

column1: With a view to effecting economy in the armed services, it is further recommended that all branches review, before the end of 1946, or, as early thereafter as possible, the need of retention of consumable stores, particularly with respect to the building up of reserves of clothing and equipment, bearing in mind the present shortage of many lines required for civilian consumption.
It is also recommended that a review should be made of post-war requirements.

Your committee recommends that a similar committee be appointed immediately after the opening of the next session. In this connection, it is respectfully suggested that study be given to the advisability of merging the work of this committee with that of the standing committee on public accounts by broadening its reference to include all war expenditures, and that the committee be known as the special committee on national expenditures.

Your committee wishes to express its appreciation of the cooperation and assistance received throughout its deliberations, from officials of War Assets Corporation, representatives of the armed services and other departmental officials.
A copy of the minutes of .proceedings and evidence taken by your committee, consisting of 1130 pages, is annexed hereto.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Gordon B. Isnor,
Chairman.",,,,

1440201,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.8.1.1.1,1946-08-17,,,,stagedirection,,,,"The house resumed, from Friday, August 2, consideration in committee of bill No. 250, respecting judges of dominion and provincial courts-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) : When this bill was before the committee on August 2, all the clauses with the exception of 27 had been passed and 27 was allowed to stand for further consideration. Clause 27 is the one which amends a former clause in the Judges Act which had to do with the possibility of the chief commissioner or the deputy chief commissioner of the board of railway commissioners, if he was a judge of the high court before appointment, being treated in the same way as if he had remained with the high court until the date of retirement from the board of railway commissioners. Section 27 proposes to extend that to other offices under the crown.

The section is of course not an integral part of the Judges Act, and it met with considerable opposition and criticism in the house. I endeavoured to redraft it in a manner to restrict it to high court judges who might be elected to the court of international justice, to high court judges who might be appointed ambassadors, or who might be appointed chief commissioner or deputy chief commissioner of the board of railway commissioners, and in the amended form I discussed it informally with some hon. members who had raised objection to the original clause. After giving it consideration they informed me that even in the modified form they felt so strongly about it that they could not allow it to pass without dividing the house on it.

I must say there are also several members on this side of the house who would naturally prefer, as I would myself, that the Judges Act have nothing to do with anything that is not strictly and essentially connected with the administration of justice, and I would also very much deprecate having a division which might be on party lines over any clause of the Judges Act. In view of the apparent overwhelming proportion of opinion in favour of all the substantial provisions of the Judges Act, and the statements that have been made to me that this clause, even in the amended form, could not pass without a division of the house, which might be on party lines, I prefer to drop both the proposed amendment and the clause, and have this act, not one sponsored by any party but one which meets the views of the large majority of members of the house regardless of party.

If it is the pleasure of the house I would ask that clause 27 be dropped, and' that would dispose of the whole act. But there is one other point that has arisen since. Hon. members will recall that the act provides for increasing by one the judges of the exchequer court and increasing by two the judges of the trial division of the supreme court of Ontario. Since the bill was before the committee we have been informed that the situation in Ontario is such that they would greatly desire to have these two additional appointments made before 1947, when the act would come into force, and I would therefore ask leaves of the house to revert to section 39 of the bill, which is the provisional section that would come into force light away, and add

The other day some mention was was made of the fact that in 1931 an amendment had been passed to make provision for the resignation of a judge from a superior court and his appointment to the railway commission in such a way that the time he was on the commission, along with the period he occupied the bench, would count in the determination of his pension I looked up that debate and found that the point which was made at that time both by Mr. Guthrie, the Minister of Justice, and Mr. Bennett, and concurred in by Mr. Lapointe, was that in the case of the chairman of the railway commission the appointment was in the nature of a judicial one, and that the railway commission was by statute a court of record.
So far as diplomatic servants are concerned I am sure the minister will be able to cover the situation by making provision that those
who serve in foreign fields shall in fact receive no less consideration than those who serve in our country.

With regard to the other amendments suggested, we of course support them. In view of the glut of work in the courts in Ontario it is necessary that these judges be appointed. We give support to the request for the amendment suggested by the Minister of Justice.

Mr. POULIOiT: Before the change is made may I say that I have a recollection of what was done some years ago by Mr. Bennett for General McNaughton. There is an analogy between what was done for him and section 27 which will disappear. He was chief of staff at a certain salary and was appointed president of the national research council at a higher salary. The position at the national research council carried no superannuation. The evidence of that is that Doctor H. M. Tory, who was president before, had nothing more than his salary. The engagement is considered a ten-year contract; but when General McNaughton was transferred from the position of chief of staff to that of president of the national research counoil he was seconded by the army to that position. In law the word ""seconded"" means that the man carries with him all the advantages that he h'ad in his previous position, even though there are no such advantages attached to the new position. Because of that seconding General McNaughton was superannuated from the national research council at a pension of $8,000 per annum instead of $4,000 and his wife will be entitled to a pension of $4,000 per annum when he dies. I am greatly surprised that that matter was not used in Qu'Appelle; it is enough to defeat a man, although it is strictly legal. Also Major General Vanier, When he was plain colonel, was secretary for a time to Howard Ferguson when he was high commissioner in England. It was a civil service position. He wias seconded by the army to that position, and he was entitled 'to more benefits. What I wanted to say is that the thing has been done by other parties in cases that were quite similar.

While I am on my feet I should like to say a word about Judge T. C. Davis, whom I know personally, and for whom I have the greatest respect. I regret some of the things that have been said about him, because in the discharge of his duties he has done exceptionally well. His name must be vindicated in the house.
Judges Act

He contributed to a large extent to making Oanadia better known in Australia, and he has done a lot for the boys who were there. I wanted to pay this tribute to him. Although I have personal views about the judiciary- and I have some very dear friends among the judges, men whom I respect very much-it does not mean that because a man is a judge he must be free from criticism when such bills- as this one come before the house. But the criticism must be fair and must be on a higher level than what took place on this bill and which could be called an aspersion on Judge Davis. It was not fair.

1440208,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.8.1.7,1946-08-17,040a15b2-afa7-4a8f-94a1-f838f850daa7,ca.m.3550,Mr. WILLIAM BRYCE (Selkirk):,,JUDGES ACT,CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.",,"While taking part in this debate previously I was asked a question by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), and I should like to take just one moment to convince the hon. member that I did know what I was talking about, though he caught me unawares at the time. We were talking about political appointments of judges in Britain, and since that time I have made a few inquiries. I am going to deal with Scotland, however, because I am more certain of my facts there than in connection with England, though in days gone by England has depended upon the good lawyers coming from Scotland to give justice there. In Scotland the judges are recommended by their brethren of the bar association; their names are submitted to the secretary for Scotland and the appointments are made official by him. That takes away entirely the political aspect of the appointment. I feel quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that this is done in England- as well. In any event they are positively not appointed because they were Liberals or Tories, but for their ability to dispense justice without bias. I might mention some of the legal lights in that class:

1440212,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.8.1.11,1946-08-17,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,JUDGES ACT,CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.",,"You have graced the bar, too.

,Progressive Conservative,,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440213,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.8.1.12,1946-08-17,f88a7275-f7f4-407e-9d45-89d5300f2919,ca.m.9510,Mr. POULIOT:,,JUDGES ACT,CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.",,"Thank you. I am quite free to express an opinion on judges, who must be considered with fairness. In the minds of the people regulations that have been passed by minor clerks are the law of the land. The private individual makes no distinction between a statute studied and approved by both houses of parliament which later receives royal sanction, and an order which is signed by a minor clerk, because the result is the same. If a citizen infringes the statutory law or the regulation he has to pay a fine or go to gaol. The other day I spoke of Gulliver; but the case of the Canadian citizen is rather different, because Gulliver did not give to. the dwarfs of Lilliput the rope with which he was tied. On the other hand we give to the dwarfs of the civil service plenty of rope with which to tie not an individual but all Canadian citizens. We supply the rope by giving them a great deal of power, and as a result the judges suffer because the necessary distinction is not made and cannot be made by the private individual unless he takes a course in law.

There is another question in my mind. The judges have to apply the law. Does that mean that the law is justice? It would be a great mistake to contend that justice and law are synonymous. I believe in equity; I believe not in the strict interpretation of the law but in its interpretation in a broad manner taking into consideration all the human facts and
Judges Act

factors related to the application of the precepts of law. Therefore we cannot very well speak any longer about the sanctity of law, except the law which derives directly from the ten commandments which ruled the world for centuries because men abided by them and followed their spirit.

There is another principle of law that the individual has no excuse for ignoring. At the present time I do not know how a candidate for legal honours can be qualified to pass successfully an examination on all the orders made during the war, which are the law of the land. At this time I must pay a special tribute to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) for his endeavour to improve conditions which could easily become chaotic in the legal domain; and he can rely on the able assistance of the Solicitor General (Mr. Jean) who for. several months has been pruning the orders in council and orders with real success. When I listened to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) a moment ago I wondered if his suggestion was that in each department the minister should dictate all the correspondence of that department. That would be beyond the physical capacity of any man, so perhaps there was a little exaggeration there. But when there is a trend in the right direction, it must be noted, approved and encouraged. In this connection I have been complaining for years about the absurdity of some of the regulations, but there is still some hope when we see the work being done under the Minister of Justice by the Solicitor General, and I congratulate them both.

,Independent Liberal,,Jean-François Pouliot,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f88a7275-f7f4-407e-9d45-89d5300f2919&Language=E&Section=ALL

1440223,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.8.1.22,1946-08-17,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,JUDGES ACT,CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.",,"Mr. Speaker, the main provisions of the bill now before us have to do with increasing the salaries of judges. We in this group have listened to the arguments that have been put forward but we remain unconvinced that it is urgent that such steps be taken at this time. As we have indicated previously, we are in favour of raising the standard of living of all Canadians, and we would not except judges from that view, but there is such a thing as priorities. We feel very strongly that for this parliament to pass the measure at this time and to fail to deal with such an important matter as old age pensions would be a disgrace. We have stated that position before, and in spite of the arguments that have been offered in support of this bill we do not feel that this is the time for it to be given third reading.

Various arguments have been put forward in favour of increasing these salaries, such as the contention that it is necessary to pay higher salaries in order to get the best men on the bench and to assure that we shall have judges who will be perfectly fair. As we said before, we regard this argument as something of a reflection upon those who hold or aspire to this high office. We feel that impartial and fair judgments are not to be obtained by paying for them. Surely a measure such as this can wait until some of these other matters of greater urgency are dealt with.

The proposal was made that something should be done this year about old age pensions. On June 24 we thought we had a promise from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) that a measure would be brought before the house relating to the amount of the old age pension. When I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) about that on July 5 he asked for time to answer, and a week later indicated that in view of the intention to introduce an amendment to the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, any legislation respecting old age pensions would have to wait until next year. During the weeks and months we have been discussing these matters the cost of living has gone up and other difficulties facing the old age pensioners have increased. We feel very keenly that our scale of values is all wrong if we go ahead with this measure and then
in a week or so prorogue without dealing with the case of the old age pensioners and others we might mention.

I would also mention the argument that was advanced in another place-I do not refer to the senate, but to a room between here and the senate-that any increase in wages of over ten cents an hour is not to be considered at the present time because it would be a threat of inflation. If that argument is valid it applies to these increases as well.

For these reasons we feel that now is not the time to give a third reading to this measure, and therefore, so as not to take any more time on it, I now move, seconded by my deskmate the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson):

I am sure that with the exhaustive work of the committee, and the tremendous amount of correspondence that members of parliament have to deal with, it has been impossible for most members to read and scrutinize all the legislation that has come before us. I hope that there will be less legislation in the future. We have had too much this year; it cannot be easily digested. We have to take it for granted that this is a good bill. Members do not have the time or the opportunity to form their own opinions about it. 'It will be the law of the land; it will be the law that will bind Canadian citizens after it is passed and sanctioned. I hope that in future sessions of parliament we shall have less legislation and that we shall work as members of parliament with regard to statutory legislation in the same manner as the solicitor general has been acting with regard to orders in council and regulations. Our work is not to pass more legislation; it is to prune legislation that we now have and make it understandable and practicable, make it the best possible for all concerned.

1440243,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.9.1.3,1946-08-17,unmatched,,,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT,MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS-COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS,,I should like to ask the minister whether he

is satisfied with the amendments which have been made by the other house. Unfortunately we have not had time to study them. I wonder whether one of them does not interfere with the effectiveness of the attempt to restrain practices which are against the best interests of people in trade. I refer to page 3, line 40, where the word ""unduly"" has been inserted. Section 30 reads:
In any case where use has been made of the exclusive rights and privileges conferred by one or more patents for invention or by one or more trade marks so as:

column2: unduly to limit the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any article or commodity which may be a subject of trade or commerce; or

column1: And this is the place where ""unduly"" has been inserted. The paragraph will now read:
unduly to restrain or injure trade or commerce in relation to any such article or commodity.

It seems to me that the word ""unduly"" limits the commissioner to some extent. I am afraid of the word ""unduly,"" because the use of patents in this country is a matter which must receive serious consideration of the combines investigation organization. A few days ago I had a protest from a retailer who wanted to import and sell certain types of radios. He found that he could neither import nor sell, neither could an organization in the United States with safety send into this country their product because they must pay certain dues to an organization in Canada known as Canadian Radio Patents Limited. For years I have known this to be the practice. On one occasion a local teacher bought in the United States a radio for a car and a little radio for his room, brought them into this country and declared them at the port of entry. Shortly afterwards he was notified by this organization that he must not use these radios in his car or in his dwelling without first of all paying an imposition to this organization. I want to be assured that this bill has in no respect been emasculated by the gentlemen of the other place.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I fully shared the hon. gentleman's concern when I went before the committee of the other place to discuss with them the terms of the bill. With respect to the word ""unduly"" which is inserted here, I do not think it makes any difference in the real meaning of the section. The word ""unduly"" would be quite unnecessary if we had only ""to injure trade,"" because to injure trade is always undue. But it was argued there, and I could not deny it, that every patent does permit some restriction of trade. So having

the word ""restrain"" they felt that the word ""unduly"" should precede it, that it should be only when one went beyond what was intended by parliament to be the proper use of a patent that he should be interfered with.

1440271,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.11.1.1,1946-08-17,,,,stagedirection,,,,PRESENTATION OP SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
The house having reverted to the order: Presenting reports by standing and select committees:
Mr. MAURICE LALONDE (Labelle) presented the second report of the committee on industrial relations, as follows:
Pursuant to the following order of reference dated 16th July, 1946, namely,

That the said committee be directed and empowered to investigate, immediately, all issues connected with and appertaining to the present industrial unrest in Canada, with power to call and examine witnesses under oath, and with power to call for persons, papers and records and take all essential evidence, and to report their findings and conclusions to the house;
And that the said committee be empowered to sit while the house is sitting, and that the said committee be further empowered to employ counsel to assist them in their deliberations,
your committee immediately commenced its sittings, and held forty-eight meetings as the exigencies of the session permitted.

It was apparent to your committee that the present industrial unrest in Canada creates a condition of emergency necessitating the immediate investigation of all issues connected with and appertaining thereto.

An opportunity was thus afforded for the first time for labour and management to present to a committee of parliament such statements as the terms of your order of reference required and such are on record.

In addition your committee heard evidence from responsible officials of the wartime prices and trade board, the national war labour board and the minister and other officials of the Department of Labour, as well as the acting Minister of Finance.
The following witnesses testified before the committee, namely,
C. H. Millard, Canadian national director, United Steelworkers of America,
H.
column2: G. Hilton, president, the Steel Company of Canada Limited, Hamilton, Ontario.

column1: Gordon MacMillan, director, Algoma Steel Corporation, Limited, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.
Clement Anson, general manager. Sydney steel plant division, Dominion Steel & Coal Corporation, Sydney, Nova Scotia.
The Honourable Mr. Justice W. D. Roach. Donald Gordon, chairman, wartime prices and trade board, Ottawa, Ontario.
C. A. L. Murchison, alternate chairman, national war labour board, Ottawa, Ontario.
Arthur MacNamara, deputy Minister of Labour, Ottawa, Ontario.
A. J. Brown, vice-chairman, wartime labour relations board, Ottawa, Ontario.
M. M. MacLean, director of industrial relations, Department of Labour, Ottawa. Ontario.
Honourable D. C. Abbott, acting Minister of Finance, Ottawa, Ontario.
Mr. Pat Conroy, chairman of the wage coordinating committee of the Canadian congress of labour.
Supply-Transport
Honourable Humphrey Mitchell, Minister of Labour, Ottawa, Ontario.
Joseph MacKenzie, United Rubber Workers of America.
George Burt, director, region 7 (UAW-CIO), Windsor, Ontario.
C. S. Jackson, Canadian president, United Electrical Workers of America, Toronto, Ontario.
This is the first time that all these points of view could be placed before a committee of parliament and the Canadian people.

The committee appointed L. W. Brockington, K.C., as mediator to discuss their respective points of view with the companies and the union. Mr. Brockington reported that while he had succeeded in meeting with the parties jointly and while further oilers were made by the parties nevertheless a settlement of the steel strike was not effected.
Your committee, in the light of the evidence heard makes the following recommendations:

column2: (a) That the proposed dominion-provincial labour conference be called at the earliest possible moment to draft a labour code within the limits of the Canadian constitution and with a view to establishing machinery for the prevention of dislocations in industry';
That in the interval much closer contact

column1: be established between the wartime prices and trade board and the regional and national war labour boards.

column2: That matters coming before the regional and national war labour boards be handled expeditiously.
Your committee is convinced that continued price control is only possible with a reasonable measure of wage control.
Your committee recommends that a measure of union security should follow certification.
Law being the basis of our society, your committee condemns:
the policy adopted by some unions and some employers of disregarding the legal machinery provided for adjusting wages and settling disputes;
breaches of the law of Canada by the use of physical force or otherwise either by employer or union.

Your committee recommends that the law of picketing be studied_ with a view to its modernization and clarification and for the purpose of making it more effective for the protection of the rights of all elements in the community.

Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may. at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
Your committee recommends that the controllers appointed by order in council P.C. 2901 be instructed to implement the terms of such order with such modifications as the government may determine.

column1: A copy of the minutes of proceedings and evidence taken before your committee as well as the exhibits filed is appended.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport):,Minister of Transport,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,"I should like to clear up some questions that were asked yesterday. The hon. member for Charlotte referred to a deduction that had been made from the salary of a lighthouse keeper in his constituency, whose name he gave. A thorough search has been made in connection with the matter brought up by the hon. member concerning deduc->

tions at Navy island bar light station, and no record can be found nor any explanation offered for the assertion that a deduction was made of $15 per month for rent. The present lightkeeper is now on retiring leave. I can give details of his salary, but I would prefer not to put them on Hansard. These details are clearly indicative that no charge or deduction has been made for rent. If the hon. member desires to see them, they are available.

The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg asked a question about the construction of a radio beacon at Cross island. The reply with reference to the lighthouse establishment at Fort Point, Liverpool harbour, is that the light is functioning as usual but the lighthouse structure is being encroached upon by erosion. The immediate site is owned by the Department of Transport, and the adjacent property,
Supply-Transport

a park, is understood to be municipally owned. Negotiations have taken place with the parks branch, Department of Mines and Resources, to ascertain if they were disposed to spend any money in protecting this site, and a negative reply was received.

The arresting of erosion is always expensive and somewhat doubtful as to final results. A thorough study is being made of the situation and of the possibility of a smaller and more modern establishment being erected, somewhat in from the waterfront, is being considered.

The hon. member for Cumberland asked a question about the light at Pugwash. The answer is that at Pugwash harbour there are two ranges and two lights in operation, one east of the harbour at Steven Point, and one west of the harbour at Bigelow. There is no change at Steven Point. At Bigelow the back light was destroyed by fire on August 11, 1942, and a temporary pole light was installed on August 15, 1942. The permanent establishment became effective in May, 1943. There is no change. The same lights are in effect as were in use in pre-war days.

I would like to clarify a reply that I made to a question asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert. I told him last evening that the sum of $236,300 had been the cost of operating ice breakers on the St. Lawrence last year. That is true, but the two vessels, the Lapointe and the MacLean, are used for other purposes as well as ice breaking, and the amount that I gave was the total amount for ice-breaking and the other work performed by the Lapointe and the MacLean. I am informed that the actual cost of ice-breaking performed by the Lapointe and the MacLean in the St. Lawrence in the fiscal year 1945-46 ,was $108,000.

,Liberal,,Lionel Chevrier,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e2b15c2f-35a6-4e4e-8e52-a4357fdebc0d&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440280,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.3,1946-08-17,4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1,ca.m.6010,Mr. STIRLING:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,May I be permitted to ask a question on a railway matter under this item?-I do not know where else to ask it. It is based on a report recently published by the British Columbia government with regard to the inquiry made by the committee on resources. It deals with the probable extension of the Pacific Great Eastern from Quesnel to Hudson Hope. The minister is well' aware of the possibilities of settlement which will result from the continuation of that road. Can the minister say whether the federal government would be ready to cooperate with the government of British Columbia to assist in making available the finances .necessary for the extension of this railway? The minister will remember that it has been the subject of consideration by the two transportation companies, by the provincial government and

by the dominion government in years past, and it would really seem as if there was a prospect of some progress being made. In view of the desire for the settlement of returned men on suitable locations and with the opportunities which will be needed for the settlement of immigrants when they begin to come, it is most desirable that assistance be given to this prospect if it be possible.

I think the only way in which I can answer the question is this. When the legislature of British Columbia asked this government to appoint representatives on a committee to study this question, we consented on certain conditions. The committee came to certain conclusions, presented in the report, one of which was that until the traffic has increased to considerably more than it is at present-I believe 1,000,0000 tons per annum was the requirement^-there would be no reason for extending the Pacific Great Eastern north to Hudson Hope.

1440304,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.27,1946-08-17,e2b15c2f-35a6-4e4e-8e52-a4357fdebc0d,ca.m.9148,Mr. CHEVRIER:,Minister of Transport,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Well, the hon. gentleman asked the question and I am going to reply to him. The hon. gentleman seeks to create the impression in this house that the deficits in
IMr. Jackman.]

connection with the Hudson Bay railway are so huge that if they were discontinued we would get relief from taxation. My hon. friend might well speak of other operations which result in deficits. There is not only the ' railway to the Hudson >bay or the elevator at the port of Churchill; there are other agencies under federal jurisdiction which show budgetary deficits. It is unfortunate * that they cannot be made to pay. I hope that some time it will be possible for us to devise ways and means whereby surpluses instead of deficits will be forthcoming on the Hudson Bay railway.

My hon. friend has asked a question on the present position and the policy in that connection. He asked the very same question last year. He asked too that this whole matter De submitted to the committee on, railways and shipping, although it had not been the practice to do that in the past. At his request I suggested that the matter be referred to the committee on railways and shipping, and there was an opportunity of discussing it fully. But my recollection is that he asked very few questions on it. I have, however, obtained a report from the research and development branch of the Canadian National Railways concerning the operation of the Hudson Bay railway, and I would refer to it in part. The report was made by Mr. S. W. Fairweather, vice-president of research and development, Canadian National Railways. He says in part that he has taken occasion to go into this matter even to the extent of limiting train service to the summer months, and if that were done it would be possible to reduce the deficit by some $175,000 a year. But to accomplish this result would be to handicap seriously the commercial development which has taken place along the line. In the report he goes on to say that mining development has, since the end of the war, taken on a new impetus in the area. He also refers to the cutting of pulpwood along the Hudson Bay railway as a new venture which he thinks will be profitable, and he concludes his report by stating in part:

I have reached the conclusion that present and prospective developments on the first two subdivisions, namely, from The Pas to Gillam. a distance of 326 miles, are such as to justify the continuance of the present train service and *when developments in the Herb lake area take place, which are planned for this year, train service on the first subdivision from The Pas to Webowden, will likely have to be increased, so that it would not be true economy to reduce the services at the present time, even though they are being operated at a loss. I am not so dear as to the justification for continuing the winter service to Churchill. The economy which might be effected by limiting the service beyond Gillam
Supply-Transport

during the winter months might be of the order of $50,000 per year, but could hardly exceed that figure. Having regard to the above, I am satisfied that the Hudson Bay railway is being operated with a minimum of expenditure consistent with the objective of furnishing enough transportation to permit of the development of the natural resources tributary to it. With the development of a mine or mines in the Herb lake area there should be some improvement in operating results.

I may say to my hon. friend, though he knows it, that the Hudson Bay railway is operated by the Canadian National Railways, and they have been doing a pretty fair job. But because of the very short supply situation it would be impossible to move further wheat to Churchill from the 1945 crop, and it is really doubtful if supplies from the 1946 crop could be moved in time to be available for shipment, that is if tonnage were available. I think hon. gentlemen will agree that if a substantial stock of wheat from the new crop were moved to Churchill and had to be housed there until August of next year, when the navigation season opens, there might be considerable criticism in view of the world demand for all possible grain to be shipped at the earliest possible moment.

The elevator capacity at Churchill is 2,200,000 bushels, and the present stores are indicated as 1,800,000 bushels. Some six ships have been made available to take out this wheat. I have before me the schedule of vessels for grain loadings at Churchill. One of these ships, the Mount Revelstoke Park, arrived on August 10 and departed on August 15, carrying 335,000 bushels of wheat. The Hillcrest Park arrived on the 12th, the Essex Trader on the 13th, the Rocky Mountain Park on the 15th, and two others, the Whiteshell Park and the Bellwood Park, have not yet arrived but are expected on the 19th and 21st respectively. These ships have a carrying capacity of 8,500 tons, and it is expected that this shipping will take care of the grain now in the elevator.

I am mentioning this in the hope that the minister will endeavour to have those who have the contract put on miore men. I do not think they are held up for materials at the present time, or at least W'e have no information on that. The boat could have been built five years ago in the United States. When the SS. Charlottetown was lost in June, 1941, the United States had not yet declared war and there was plenty of opportunity to have this ship built in their shipyards. However, that has been lost to us and Prince Edward Island has been a greater sufferer thereby.

In dealing with this matter, I do not want to say anything that is unfair in any way. I simply wish to place before the minister the terrible conditions with regard to shipping in Prince Edward Island. Our farmers have already become very uneasy with regard to the shipments they expect to make this coming season. I hold in my hand a copy of a letter dated July 12, 1946, which was sent to the Prime Minister by the potato growers' association, drawing to his attention what they are looking for by way of having this ship completed for 1946, and among other things, they say, in conclusion:
We respectfully urge you, honourable sir, that you as head of all departments will see that every possible effort is made to have the new ferry reach us in time for the traffic of this coming winter.
There have been all kinds of representations made to the department, all urging the early completion of this ship.

Another thing that has tied up our transportation facilities and given our tourist business a black eye has been what I might call the neglect with regard to the repairs to the Prince Edward, a ship which has been in service all winter. We know that she had to be repaired, and after she had gone in for repairs we were furnished with an auxiliary ship at the beginning of the tourist season. Just when the tourists were starting to come in many of them could not get across the strait on time and had to sleep in their cars all night on the Tormentine side. The government of Prince Edward Island spends some $25,000 a year in advertising for tourist business, but any friends they make in that way are simply wiped off the map by the delays of the dominion government. The whole thing seems to be more or less of a muddle and we can get no satisfaction as to when we can depend on the new ship being in service.
May I draw to the attention of the committee the opinion of the premier of Prince
Edward Island regarding this matter. In a speech in the local legislature in March last he said:

It seems to me that under the terms of confederation, when something has happened to interrupt our communication for which the dominion failed to make adequate provision, we have a claim against Canada for the loss sustained. The delay of even a day or two might bring up claims of thousands of dollars. I believe that we should claim from the dominion government, on account of delinquencies on their part for transportation across the straits, hundreds of thousands of dollars-it may be millions.
column2: [DOT]

column1: That is from the Liberal premier of our province. Our people in Prince Edward Island are most anxious to-day because the situation is so serious. Here we are with the expectation of shipping at least 9,000 to 10,000 cars of potatoes this fall. That is quite a lot to be carried over by the one steamer. Should we have to hold over some of that crop until the winter season and should the old ship happen to break down, look what a loss that would be to our farmers!

I might state further that, because of the hold-up this summer, the coal shortage has become almost desperate there; and with coal to come in, and the shortage of refrigerator cars for potatoes, we are going to have a real bottleneck in transportation in Prince Edward Island. The minister may think I am simply making complaints, but I am not making these representations by way of complaint at all. I simply wish to place before the committee and the minister how serious the transportation situation is there, in the hope of arousing his very best interest. I am sure that if he will look into the matter we shall have his support and that our shippers and our whole transportation system will benefit.

column2: Canadian government railways - Construction and improvements of drainage works at Fairview subway, at Halifax, N.S.-capital, $40,000.",,,,

column1: 1440373,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.95,1946-08-17,58a4a9e8-42c9-4fe6-b9ae-c18e764d9a45,ca.m.2972,Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,"This vote will, I hope, help to end a menace and a nuisance that has existed in Halifax since 1916 when the Fairview subway was built as part of the Halifax ocean terminals project. It is the main exit out of the city of Halifax, and it presents two problems, one having to do with flooding and the other with the passage of traffic. The vote here is for the construction of improvements to drainage works at Fairview. It is quite true that flood conditions there, following torrential rains, render this subway impassable at times, but there is also great danger to traffic moving to and from the subway, in and out of the city. What I wish to inquire about is whether this vote will cover not only drainage and improvements but also improvements to the subway, so that it will help to make the passageway safer for traffic. It is a problem which concerns not only the Canadian government railways but the department of highways of the Nova Scotia government and, as well, the city of Halifax. All three parties should be interested in the work to be done, and I would ask the minister whether he has the approval and concurrence of the provincial highways department and the city of Halifax for the proposed work.

Perhaps I might put on record just what we have done in the Department of Transport for lighthouse keepers; and I think I can be brief. There is a definite trend in the department to improve the condition of lightkeepers, who, it is recognized, are faithful servants of the crown. As my hon. friend knows, an order in council was passed and some $40,000 voted yesterday, covering an additional allowance for lighthouse keepers to assist toward paying the wages of assistants at the rate of $25 a month. . In addition to the cost of living bonus, the principle of annual leave for lightkeepers has been recognized, and it is being extended and generally made available with pay where stations are in operation the year round. Housing is being improved, with sanitary conditions being incorporated in new structures and added to others, and we are trying to get separate accommodation for assistants. Radiotelephones are being installed on both coasts, which it is hoped will be in operation this fall. Where reasonably available, electricity is being installed, and also telephone service. Every possible assistance is given by the marine service steamers, and their visits augmented by mail service contracts where that is possible. Consideration is being given to the department assuming other assistance and other benefits for the lightkeepers.

My hon. friend spoke of the light at Cape Mudge. Until recently this was a single man station, but the classification has been raised to provide for an assistant. I am instructed that winding is rarely required more frequently than every four hours. At most single-man stations the winding is arranged for every fourteen hours, according to my information from the director of marine services.

1440431,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.152,1946-08-17,58a4a9e8-42c9-4fe6-b9ae-c18e764d9a45,ca.m.2972,Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I think the time has come when we should have a Canadian maritime commission. I believe that such a commission would be in the interests of both the ship owners and the seamen. It could assist in securing regular and permanent employment for the ships of our merchant fleet and also for our seamen. I have in my hand a copy of the merchant marine act, 1936, passed by the United States congress which provides for a United States maritime commission. The declaration of policy is set out in the first section, which provides:

It is necessary for the national defence and development of its foreign and domestic commerce that the United States shall have a merchant marine (a) sufficient to carry its domestic water-borne commerce and a substantial portion of the water-borne export and import foreign commerce .of the United States and to provide shipping service on all routes essential for maintaining the flow of such domestic and foreign water-borne commerce at all times; (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency; (c) owned and operated under the United States flag by citizens of the United States in so far as may be practicable and (d) composed of the best equipped, safest, and most suitable types of vessels, constructed in the United States and manned with a trained and efficient citizen personnel.

Section 210 of the act provides that it shall be the duty of the commission set up under the act to make a survey of the United States merchant marine with a view to securing, among other things, a merchant fleet owned by citizens of the United States and to plan vessels designed to afford the best and most complete protection for passengers and crew against fire and all marine perils.

Another section provides that the commission is authorized and directed to study all maritime problems arising in the carrying out of the policy set forth in the act and to study and cooperate with vessel owners in devising means by which the importers and exporters of the United States can be induced to give preference to vessels under United States registry.

To-day Canada is a great trading nation. At the outbreak of war we had thirty-seven ocean-going ships, with a total personnel of about 1,400. To-day we have over 200 oceangoing vessels, with a personnel of 12,000 trained seamen. Prior to the war, it seemed to be taken for granted that it was impossible for Canada to have a strong merchant marine. Most of our exports and imports were carried in bottoms of [DOT] United Kingdom or foreign registry. In those days we were not in position to look after our merchant ships as we are to-day.

At the present time there is a wide demand all over the world for Canadian products. Before the war-and I suppose this custom still exists-the purchaser of goods would dictate the ship in which those goods were to be carried. To-day we are making loans and advancing credits to many countries, and it seems to me that the time has come when we should see that the goods and commodities purchased as a consequence of these credits and advances should be shipped in Canadian ships sailing from Canadian ports.

It is no use to say that the adoption of such a policy would mean that orders would be placed in the United States instead of in Canada. That answer was given me a year ago when I brought up this question. Ten years ago the United States congress passed a law which requires that all exports financed by government money shall be carried in ships registered in the United States if there are sufficient ships of sufficient tonnage available. There is no good reason why we should not adopt the same policy.

There is another matter that might very well be considered by a maritime commission. It is one that has arisen at different times. That is the question of restricting our coastal trade to Canadian ships. That is the policy followed in the United States. Much of our coastal trade is being carried by foreign ships owned in countries where the same privileges are not given to our ship owners.

Another matter that might very well be considered by this commission is safety provisions for the crew and passengers of ships, crew accommodation and better services in the kitchens or galleys in order to make life at sea safer and more pleasant. This commission could absorb some of the activities of the Canadian shipping board, which was set up in 1939 under the War Measures Act and whose existence I presume will soon come to an end. That board did excellent work during the war. I have heard criticism of its work in no part of the country.
We find ourselves in this position. We have in Canada a large merchant fleet of over
Supply-Transport

200 vessels, employing over 14,000 seamen. We are well equipped with ships; we have the material, the means and the personnel in Canada to build ships. Many thousands of our men are skilled iu the art of shipbuilding. We should not lose those skills and that important trade. Our national economy W'ould suggest that steps be taken now to ensure the continued employment of all these classes of men. We have many different departments to-day concerned with the problems of seamen, shipbuilding and shipping, and I think the time has come when all these activities should be coordinated. I know of no better way of doing that than by setting up a maritime commission and having it study all these problems and be in a position to advise the government. I do not say that such a commission should be given all the powers given to the commission in the United States, but many of those powers might well be adapted to this country. I would ask the minister to give his favourable consideration to this suggestion.

,Liberal,,William Chisholm Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=58a4a9e8-42c9-4fe6-b9ae-c18e764d9a45&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440432,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.153,1946-08-17,f88a7275-f7f4-407e-9d45-89d5300f2919,ca.m.9510,Mr. POULIOT:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Before the minister replies, I wish to congratulate my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax upon his excellent speech. But I wonder if this work should be done by a commission. I am a strong believer in having a large number of Canadian ships to carry Canadian produce. The mail contracts should also be given to ships of Canadian registry. That would be a great inducement to shipping companies to register their ships in Canada. Then they would be under the control of the Minister of Transport. That is most important, because many a time ships of foreign registry do some wrong to Canadian shipping and get away from the jurisdiction of the minister.

I support wholeheartedly my hon. friend's suggestion that we should build a large fleet of merchant ships of our own, and I would suggest that the government see that we get the largest possible number of ships to take care of our foreign trade so that there will be no delay in making shipments. That is a thing that cannot be done all at once; it may take some time, but it should be done. In this matter we should leave aside the old school tie of past ages. Our business in foreign countries is now in charge of commercial attaches who are responsible to British authorities and sometimes are not free and independent. The only thing they do is to make some reports and answer letters that are sent to them. They must be more active than that, and they must be under Canadian jurisdiction, because trade is the life-blood of the nation. If the views expressed by the junior
member for Halifax are carried out, I believe it will be to the great benefit of this country.

There is something in the air, Mr. Chairman. What was said not long ago in another debate shows that there is a change of mind for the better in some quarters of the house and that some are now prepared to consider Canadian interests first. That is of the utmost importance because, if we cannot develop our own trade, this country is finished.

,Independent Liberal,,Jean-François Pouliot,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f88a7275-f7f4-407e-9d45-89d5300f2919&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440433,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.154,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The Minister of Transport has asked me to reply since I have been charged by the government with the duty of exploring the possibilities of a maritime commission and of reporting to the government on the requirements. There seems to be little doubt that Canadian shipping at the moment is in the position where a maritime commission is required.

The functions mentioned by my hon. friend are being taken care of to-day by three different departments. For example, the Canadian shipping board and shipping subsidies are administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce; the regulation of shipping is in the Department of Transport; and the operation of Park Steamships Company and certain control of shipyards is centred in the Department of Reconstruction.

Some progress is being made in drafting a maritime act to be administered by a maritime commission. The sale of Park Steamships Company has been carried out with a view to building a substantial Canadian merchant marine, and an endeavour has been made to place our shipyards in a position to service a substantial Canadian maritime fleet. There has not been great urgency about the formation of a maritime commission to date, because our ships and shipyards have been busy on foreign orders. However, the situation may change shortly, and for that reason we hope that some time next year we shall have a maritime commission in operation.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

1440435,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.156,1946-08-17,b3e9b269-147a-4272-9fea-5a61707135db,ca.m.7425,Mr. MERRITT:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,"Last year, at page 2495 of Hansard, the Minister of Reconstruction highly praised the proposed air service between Vancouver and Lethbridge, stopping at intermediate points in the interior of British Columbia. In part, he said this:

This is considered an excellent aeroplane route. The rail transportation, as I think my hon. friend will agree, is not the best, and weather conditions are such that from time to time the highways are blocked. Another fortunate feature is that the area is well supplied
Supply-Air Service
with airports, so that a well-equipped and well-financed company should be able to give an excellent service and should find it a profitable operation.

At the same time he referred to the application by three companies to the air transport board which was heard in Vancouver in January, to operate over this line. Recently the application of each of the three companies has been turned down, and apparently the air transport board will not permit any company to operate this route at the present time and under present conditions.

The air transport board turned down the application on five grounds. They said first that the traffic potential of the area was not enough. My only comment on that is that, if that rule is to be applied by the board, we shall not have any scheduled intermediate service lines in British Columbia for many a long day, because this route passes through the most populated part of British Columbia. In the interior will be found a population of over 150,000; the Vancouver area contains some 400,000 and upwards; and the Lethbridge area, some 25.000. If that kind of thing is going to stop the approval of the service we shall have to wait for a long time in British Columbia before we have such a service. Next, the air transport board found that the rail and the bus services were quite adequate. I just read what the minister's view of that is, and my view is exactly the same as that of the minister. The third ground of the air transport board's decision was that the weather was so bad that the route could not be operated on schedule. There again, if we are to change the weather before we have any kind of scheduled service to these points we shall have to wait much longer than the people of Canada and particularly the people of the area concerned will want. Fourthly, it was said that the operation of this route would not be undertaken at a loss. Of course that is certainly so; nobody will want to operate such a route at a loss. The fifth reason given was that the aeroplane DC-3 was obsolescent, was not operationally satisfactory for the route, and was too large. Well, I understand the DC-3 to be the wartime Dakota, and I would think it most surprising to most people who know anything about air service to say that the DC-3 was Obsolescent enough to make that a factor in washing out the service, particularly since I understand that the T.C.A. is now equipping certain of its services with that self-same aircraft.
But the real reason this application was turned down was not mentioned by the air transport board. It was that the company

had applied for fifty cents per mile airmail subsidy and the department had offered only fifteen cents per mile of such subsidy. They later brought that offer up to 22i cents per mile, but it was considered by the companies concerned that it was impossible to inaugurate this service without fifty cents per mile, the calculations being worked out on carrying a minimum of five passengers per mile and the rest of the cost being made up in the initial stages by the airmail subsidy. The rate of fifteen cents is, as I understand, the present established rate for T.C.A. It has been reduced to this figure very recently: the minister will know the exact date; I am not sure, but I believe it is since the end of the war. Before that time, T.C.A. was getting an airmail subsidy of forty-two cents per mile, and when T.C.A. was first inaugurated it got sixty cents per mile. It is again my understanding, subject to correction by the minister, that private airline companies which have received airmail subsidies in the past have received them to the amount of sixty cents, or fifty cents, or something comparable with the T.C.A. rate.

My first complaint to the committee and to the minister is that a mail subsidy to a transportation company has historically been a wiay of getting a necessary service into operation, and I do not believe that there has been a transportation system in the world for a hundred years^-and probably one could go back much further than that-which has not had some assistance in the way of mail subsidies from the government to get it ""over the hump.""

Here we have a situation where we have thousands of men coming back from overseas qualified to serve in this particular walk of life, which is important for Canadians in the future, and we find a complete change of policy by the government in this respect. Apparently, from now on. the airmail subsidies which will be offered will be only in the amount which a well established and well cared for air line like the T.CA., with all the advantages it has, is allowed. If we are to have an expansion of flying in this country to the extent that we should have it, a change of policy of that kind is a serious thing to face. I do not think the committee will doubt that if the T.C.A. determine to expand1 or to institute any service they will get all the money they need to do it and they will get any subsidy they need to do it. The minister said, talking about this very business last year, that if a service were necessary he would be in favour of giving it a subsidy. So that to come along, after blowing up the route in this
Supply-Air Service

house, after saying that one of these companies would be chosen for this route, after letting them incorporate, letting them make all their arrangements, encouraging them to come forward, and then bring in this new and this bad policy, is particularly hard on the companies concerned and very hard on air transport generally in Canada.

I do not intend to go into the details of this particular operation because, while my remarks are, of course, directed to this case, they will be equally applicable to every other company which is interested in developing private routes. There is great need for a clear indication by the minister of the scope that will be given private schedule services in this country. We had this matter up last session, and all hon. members will recall the long debate on bush and feeder lines and the evasive answers-I use that word advisedly- of the minister with respect to what he would permit. There is need for definition of the airmail subsidies policy. There is need for the institution of a policy at a more or less higher rate at the inception of an air line and then a scaled-down rate as it gets going. That is the practice followed in the past in all modes of transportation and the practice followed in Canada in particular by this government in relation to the development of air lines. There is great need for the drawing of a line between T.C.A. and other companies, because the minister can hardly expect many people in the country not to believe that, if the kind of thing that I have raised here goes on, there is a desire on the part of the government to keep competition with T.C.A. off these intermediate lines and to reserve them for eventual development by T.C.A., thus in effect holding from the people who require it a necessary service until T.C.A. comes along to do the work.

There is another and perhaps the most important definition of policy which the minister must give, and that is whether the transport board is to decide these questions on their merits or on instructions from the government. Here we have a perfectly clear case where the air transport board turns down an application on five technical grounds related to the safety and the possibilities of development of the route, none of which holds water in the minds of the people interested. Then we find that behind that decision of the board was the real reason, that the government was not going to provide airmail subsidies which these people had every right to expect when they started on their venture. It seems to me to be more than clear that this decision of the air transport board has been dictated by the minister and the board has had to produce reasons to get round the difficulty.
The same thing, many hon. members believe, is going on in connection with radio, and no doubt other examples can be given.

The last thing I want to say about this case is that one can see in it the heavy hand of regulation by the government. These counsels of perfection which the government seems to require should be applied only to a reasonable extent necessary for safety of life. A little initiative should be left to the discretion of those who are to put their money into the project. We would then have a very much faster development of air transport in the country, to the great good of all those who wish to travel and also to the great good of those people who are keen to get into this game and to make use of the skill they have acquired in recent years.

I urge the minister to reconsider the question of airmail subsidies and to recognize that they are subsidies for development, and have always been such, and to give private companies that wish to fly such services the same opportunity as he will undoubtedly give T.C.A.

,Progressive Conservative,,Charles Cecil Ingersoll Merritt,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b3e9b269-147a-4272-9fea-5a61707135db&Language=E&Section=ALL
