1440447,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.168,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Thank you. The route was advertised by the air transport board. It believed it to be a good route and it received three applications. The board would have been glad to grant a licence to any one of the three had it been able to assure the board that it could operate the route on the traffic in view and the rates offered. The three applicants filed their rates for various services, with which there was no quarrel. Passenger rates were higher than charged by Trans-Canada Air Lines, but no exception was taken to that. It was believed that the rates were in line with the requirements of the traffic. The difficulty was that, when all other means of revenue were added up, a certain amount was required for carriage of mail to make the operation balance out and show a profit. I have nothing to do with the arrangements with the post office. The responsible officers went to the Post Office Deparment and applied for a certain rate. The Post Office Department replied that all it could grant was the Trans-Canada rate, which is a pound rate for the carriage of mail. I think the rate is 1-5 mills per pound per mile. That rate was offered to the applicants. The air transport board conducted a survey of the probable mail on the route, and that figure was given to the airways company. It was found that the revenue from mail was not nearly sufficient, and on a renewed application I think the
Post Office Department guaranteed a minimum rate of-I am not sure what the minimum rate is, I would say 150 pounds.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440448,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.169,1946-08-17,4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1,ca.m.6010,Mr. STIRLING:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,It is 100 pounds.

,Progressive Conservative,,Grote Stirling,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440449,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.170,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,One hundred pounds, which is unusual; at least there is no guarantee to any other air line that I know of; each air line simply depends on the actual mail that it obtains, but this other company got a guarantee. I personally intervened to the extent of writing my colleague to say that I hoped the Post Office Department could take another view and perhaps increase the guarantee. After a survey of its position, the Post Office Department believed that it was not justified in doing so. If Capilano Airways Limited had said that, knowing all the facts, it wished to operate the line, without subsidy, a licence would have been granted, and will be granted to-day if it cares to appeal the ruling of the board. There is no question about that. Licences are granted freely in all parts of Canada to those who can make a living out of the business there is in sight; but it is questionable policy that the provision of the Aeronautics Act concerning the subsidization of new air lines should be used for subsidizing a line which, in view of the air transport board, is not likely to be self-supporting for a considerable time.

It is all very well to subsidize the necessary services into undeveloped country if the service cannot be provided in any other way. This is being done in one instance for a service which was formerly a profitable one. On account of the closing of mining operations, it was having a difficult time, but for the services to be discontinued would have left a number of settlers without any communication whatever.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440450,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.171,1946-08-17,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. DIEFENBAKER:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The M. and C. Aviation Company.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440451,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.172,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Yes, that is the only service in the country that is being subsidized at the moment. We have a case in Nova Scotia which is at a critical stage. The Maritime Central Airways applied for a route from Saint John to Yarmouth to Halifax. It simply applied for the route. The application was granted because the indications were that the Maritime Central Airways believed that it could carry on the operation without a subsidy. No subsidy was asked for. It is found that it cannot carry on without a subsidy. It finds that it is losing money and it wants to discontinue the route. There was a hearing before the air transport board. It is asking for permission to discontinue its scheduled services. The government can hardly be expected to be in the position that anyone
Supply-Air Service
who wishes to start a route will automatically get a subsidy if the route does not show a profit.

The route proposed is over a territory which I should like to see developed. The board advertised for applications for the route, and three were submitted. Every effort has been made to explore the situation and to assist the air lines to determine whether it will be a profitable operation. I think the board is performing a service for applicants and for all concerned in seeing that the facts are fully developed. Personally I am sorry that my colleague, the Postmaster General, is not more optimistic about the mail prospects there; but he has made his investigation and has formed his opinion of the airmail potentialities. There remain the express and freight but that, of course, is a matter for development by the air line. That is a matter, I presume, on which the Capilano Airways have made their own estimate and have decided the possible revenue which can be obtained from that source.

Reference was made to the report of the air transport board. I can hardly believe that it reads, as my hon. friend says, that the DC-3 aeroplane is obsolescent; but there is a characteristic of the DC-3 aeroplane which the board believed makes it unsuitable for operation over high mountains, namely, that it has not a good single-engine performance at high altitude. Trans^Canada Air Lines has some twenty-five DC-3's and operates them everywhere in Canada except across the Rockies, for Trans-Canada Air Lines does not believe it is safe to operate them over mountainous country at altitudes above 11,000 feet. That is a technical opinion, and for that reason Trans-Canada Air Lines uses Lockheeds, which have a satisfactory single-engine performance at high altitude. I suppose the board gave its opinion as information for potential operators of the route. I just put in that word of explanation to show why that plane is not considered satisfactory.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440452,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.173,1946-08-17,b3e9b269-147a-4272-9fea-5a61707135db,ca.m.7425,Mr. MERRITT:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I wish to say to the minister that I have no personal charge to maintain at all.

,Progressive Conservative,,Charles Cecil Ingersoll Merritt,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b3e9b269-147a-4272-9fea-5a61707135db&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440453,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.174,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Why would the hon. member say that the minister dictated?

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440454,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.175,1946-08-17,b3e9b269-147a-4272-9fea-5a61707135db,ca.m.7425,Mr. MERRITT:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I am going to explain that. When I see five reasons given by the board for turning down an application and that none of these reasons apparently would hold water if the question of the mail payments is overcome, it is hard for anyone not to believe that there must have been some knowledge on the part of the air transport board that airmail payments would not be

increased, and therefore that the application would not be granted. Had the board turned it down on the ground that, since no airmail contract of the amount required could be obtained, they would not have approved it on the financial ground, then I would not have said what I said. But when they bring in technical grounds to support a position from which they would withdraw if the financial reasons were removed, I think my comment, and certainly my request that the minister say whether it is an independent board, are quite justified.

The other thing I wish to say is that in using the word ""subsidies"" with respect to the airmail contract 1 was using a word which has been in common use for a long time with regard to steamships, for instance. One often hears of airmail subsidies. Let us call them airmail contracts. I wish to point out to the committee that the amount asked by this particular airline for its airmail contract was fifty cents per mile, whereas the Trans-Canada Air Lines received at the beginning sixty cents, and forty-two cents for most of its life until now, and has only recently been dropped to fifteen cents. If that contract was good for the Trans-Canada Air Lines, why is it not good for a private company pioneering a new route?

,Progressive Conservative,,Charles Cecil Ingersoll Merritt,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b3e9b269-147a-4272-9fea-5a61707135db&Language=E&Section=ALL
1440455,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.176,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I should like to explain the airmail rates. The basis of the Trans-Canada Air Lines contract was first a rate per mile, sixty cents per mile. By a profit-sharing arrangement set out in the act that rate was reduced to forty-one cents per mile. Then the contract was changed to another basis which the Post Office Department thought was fairer, and which the Trans-Canada Air Lines was willing to accept. At present, when T.C.A. carries a pound of mail a mile it gets paid 1-5 mills for the service. T.C.A. is not subsidized; the mail it carries returns payment to it at that rate. The present rate is not a drop from forty-two cents a mile; as a matter of fact it is about the same thing. The earnings from mail this year under that contract are about the same as they were under the rate of forty-two cents a mile. The difficulty in the Okanagan is that the potential volume of mail is not heavy enough to promise a satisfactory return.

1440468,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.189,1946-08-17,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. KNOWLES:,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I should like to discuss briefly with the minister a matter pertaining to civil aviation policy in connection with
Supply-Air Service

which he and I do not see eye to eye. However, before doing this I should like to offer a word of well-deserved congratulation to the government, and more particularly to the minister, for his administration in this field. We know how proud the minister is of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and he has every reason to be proud of the efficiency and1 safety with which that line operates. He has also reason to be proud of the speed with which it has been extending its services, not only in Canada but to other co'untries and across the seas to other parts of the world.

I have a certain amount of sympathy with the general attitude of the government toward civil aviation, in that they seem to realize that this is a service to be developed. The government has seemed anxious to avoid some of the mistakes of the past, particularly in the early days of the railroads, and to provide service without the disadvantages of cut-throat competition. The minister knows that we in this group welcomed and gave strong support to the general statement of policy which he made on March 17, 1944, and to certain other statements which he made and measures which he has brought down from time to time. However, in his statement of March 17, 1944, the minister made one pronouncement which does not seem to have been carried out. He said, as recorded in Hansard:

Accordingly, after full consideration, the government has decided that the railways shall not exercise any monopoly of air services. Steps will be taken to require our railways to divest themselves of ownership of air lines, to the end that, within a period of one year from the ending of the European war, transport by air will be entirely separate from surface transportation.

The minister indicated that he was not altogether happy about having to make a break between the Canadian National and Trans-Canada Air Lines; but because of the way in which Canadian Pacific Air Lines had -and I am using his own words-""lost no time in challenging the non-competitive position of Trans-Canada Air Lines"", it was necessary to put forward this new policy. In leading up to that, he made a statement which is part of my reason for having offered a few complimentary remarks, and I quote again;
Service to the public must be the paramount consideration, and it seemed obvious that the cost of a non-competitive, non-profit service was the lowest that could be offered the public.

There are many other quotations which I could make from that excellent speech of the minister, but I shall not take the time to do so. I only wish he had lived up to it in full. Later on in that session, there was

further discussion of this proposal to compel the railways to divest themselves of ownership of air lines. I felt at the time that the minister had retreated from the forceful and aggressive position which he had taken on March 17. When I suggested to him on April 21, 1944, that he had made such a retreat he did not altogether like it. I quote his words:
I said we had better wait until we had seen the bill.
That was his reply to my charge that the minister had retreated.

So far as the complete implementing of the policy is concerned, we are still waiting, and this is now August, 1946, more than two years later. In the meantime a bill was introduced and passed, an act to amend the Aeronautics Act, Bill No. 133, of the session of 1944, which contained clauses designed to give legislative effect to this policy laid down on March 17, 1944. Section 14 of that act reads in part-I will give just the significant clause:

. . . but every such licence, if not cancelled or suspended by the board under section thirteen of this act, shall cease to be valid one year after the termination, as fixed by order in council, of the war in Europe which commenced on the tenth day of September, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine.
Another section of the same act, section 12, subsection 2, related to this matter, and reads as follows:

No such licence shall be issued in respect of a commercial air service, owned, leased, controlled or operated by any person who is en-aged in the transport of goods or passengers or hire or reward by means other than aircraft unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such licence be issued.

That bill was passed in the session of 1944. So far as I can learn, the many subsidiary companies which were bought up by the Canadian Pacific are still being operated by that company. This raises, of course, the whole question, the merits of which some might want to debate, but I remember very well that when the former member for York-Sunbury, Mr. Hanson, charged that the government's policy amounted to confiscation the minister's reply, which I heartily endorsed, was that these smaller companies which had been pioneered in the earlier days by independent operators had in effect been confiscated by the Canadian Pacific, ""which entered the field of transportation by air and bought the stock of all the independent operators, thus obtaining by the end of 1941 a monopoly in the field of transport by air except for trans-continental air lines"". I have been paraphrasing, except at the end when I was quoting the minister.
Supply-Air Service

My concern about all this is that it seems to me that we are laying the basis of another huge monopoly in the northern part of this country. The thing I am most concerned about is the monopoly of transportation in the northland which the Canadian Pacific has and of the way in which that transportation monopoly can tie in with a monopoly in mineral production in northern Canada. My whole point is that I welcomed, as all of us did in this group, the statement of policy made by the minister. We welcomed the extent to which that statement was given legislative effect in the bill from which I have just quoted. But I should now like to hear from the minister when it is to be carried out.

I suppose there may be some argument as to when the war in Europe ended, but I think it ended in May, 1945, and more than a year has since elapsed. When we were discussing that particular section, section 14, on July 17, 1944, the minister said, and I quote his words, ""My hon. friend will see that section 14 is mandatory."" That is the section which calls upon the board to cancel licences previously in effect which, as I say, made it possible to give effect to this general policy.

There are other things with regard to civil aviation about which I should like to speak if it were not for taking up the time of the committee at this stage. But I should like to hear from the minister with respect to this whole question of policy relating to the ownership of air lines by railway companies, with particular reference to Canadian Pacific Air Lines.

1440477,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.198,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The position is that we explored the possibilities of carrying out announced government policy. It seemed easy when it was announced. We thought it would be easy to divide up the system and return it to small operations, but when we undertook to do so we were faced with a great expansion of air activity in the north which required additional services. Obviously Canadian Pacific Air Lines was not in a position to buy extra equipment until it had some security of service. We then explored as to how we could break the system down into individual routes, each serving a particular territory, as was proposed at the time the discussion took place. But we could find no group strong enough to take over any of these services. The value of the equipment owned by Canadian Pacific Air Lines was in the vicinity of seven or eight million dollars. The additional equipment required ran into several more millions. I might remind my hon. friend that to-day an ordinary 20-passenger plane costs some

Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines. To-day the two operations are working as an integrated system. At the time, Canadian Pacific Air Lines was ambitious to extend its territory into other parts of Canada. To-day it finds it has a sufficient task to develop the parts of Canada for which it was then and is now responsible for giving service, with the result that any new air lines that care to enter the business and are able to finance their operation can find a scope for their activities in parts of Canada not at present served. To-day I have come to the conclusion that, while the policy when it was announced may then have been the correct policy, the public interest, which I say again must be the paramount consideration of all air line activities, is better served by the present combination of services than it could be served by any plan which can now be devised as an alternative to the present arrangement.

One does not often make predictions, because these things go on the record and they can be thrown back at you, as I have been throwing back the minister's statements to him to-day. But I declare that the day will come when we shall have -to undo the harm done to the Canadian economy by the monopoly which we are building up in transportation and mineral production in Canada's northland, which surely belongs to the people of the country as a whole.

Canadian Pacific Air Lines insists-and one has no reason to doubt their figures-that it is losing money on its air line operations, particularly those in the north. Well, I am not one who imagines that a company of that size is losing money unless it feels that there is an advantage somewhere else, or an advantage in the future which makes that loss worth while; and I am very sony to hear that the minister has changed his mind. Whether it was that pressure, or whatever it was, which caused him to change his mind I do not know. But they will be jointly responsible for the monopoly which is being built up as a result of this, and for this further exploitation of the natural resources that belong to the Canadian people, and for the harm which will yet have to be undone.

However, I am pleased that the minister has, shall we say for the 'first time, seen the light. I want to make just one reply to our socialist friends with regard to serving the public. I have in mind one mining camp which is to-day and has been served entirely by air. I speak of the Red Lake mining camp, with a population of between four and five thousand people. To put that camp in the hands of a small operator would be nothing short of criminal. At times when you have bad weather you may have as many as fifteen or twenty aircraft a day flying into that camp with vital supplies; and you must have, for camps of this kind, a thoroughly reliable, large and perfectly competent organization to do the job. 1440505,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.226,1946-08-17,3e03759e-dc20-4a10-96de-950b5dc8cd5b,ca.m.3832,Mr. SKEY:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I ask the question because I notice that under item 432 we have the administration of the Aeronautics Act and regulations. The point I wish to call to the attention of the minister is that there is at the present time a great potential in this country which may be stopped from developing our aerial companies and their abilities if the regulations are too closely followed. I refer to the instructors, engineers, pilots, radio operators. navigators and other specialists, including flying control specialists who have come back from overseas. I understand that the regulations under which they must now obtain licences are in some cases antiquated, while in other cases these returned men are required to pass examinations, for which they have already qualified in the service, but examinations such as perhaps you, Mr. Chairman, or the minister might have passed in your youth, he in engineering and you possibly in agriculture or some other line, examinations in connection with which you have forgotten a great deal though your knowledge goes well beyond that. These men are also required to go through some practical tests on machines which at times are not of modern design.

My point is this. In the United Kingdom the regulations regarding the licensing of various specialist air personnel are handled through the air ministry, and a uniform standard is set throughout the whole country. The results of the examinations, whether set by civil authorities or by air authorities, are fed into the air ministry, and the whole thing is controlled from a central point under an authority which is up to date and knows what the requirements and regulations are for the future.

I feel that at this time some men are being forced to go back and study for possibly six months before they can get a licence to be an engineer. I can quote one case which may startle the committee and the minister. There is a Pathfinder pilot who was able to pinpoint his way into Germany and - drop his bombs within 100 yards of the mark, the target for 63260-315

his aircraft following him, and yet when he came back from overseas he was not licensed to fly at night. He had a great struggle with the air transport department to get a licence to fly at night-a Pathfinder pilot from overseas!

I need say no more. The minister will readily see that there should be some tie-up between the air force and the civil aviation division, so that there may be a standardization of licensing and those men qualified in the air may immediately receive civil qualification.

,Progressive Conservative,,Lawrence Wilton Skey,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3e03759e-dc20-4a10-96de-950b5dc8cd5b&Language=E&Section=ALL

1440514,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.235,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The finest pilots in the world come out of the air force and join Trans-Canada, but they are not allowed to sit on the lefthand side of a Trans-Canada plane until they have taken, at least six or eight months of training. 1440521,ca.proc.d.1946-08-17.13.242,1946-08-17,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The air service estimates are the estimates covering the services which were carried on pre-war. The second group of services were built definitely as military services. there is such need. I happened to be out at the airport last January when there was a sudden call for this emergency hospital ship to go to a remote corner of the province. I do not think he worries very much about who is in the plane, or whether it is a civilian or military plane or a plane belonging to the Saskatchewan government. If it is the turn of the plane to take off, it takes off as soon as it can safely do so.
